# CIVILIZE THE BUSINESS SCHOOL: FOR A CIVIC MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
## LAURA A. COLOMBO University of Exeter
Management scholars have long exposed the inadequacy of management education in addressing the complex problems confronting business and society, including ecological and climate emergencies. Concerns have been expressed about the culture of competition, self-interest, greed, and short-termism that still dominates the business school, despite the irreparable ecological damage that this culture has contributed to creating, and the innumerable business scandals it has generated. To navigate the grand challenges of our time, management education needs to be shaken at its very foundations. In this essay, I unpack the process that generates these dysfunctional consequences to expose the root of the problem: assumptions of self-interest, instrumental rationality, capitalist organizing, and mechanistic worldviews generate self-fulfilling prophecies. Only once this harmful process is better understood is it possible to move beyond critique and support the virtuous cycles enabling functional outcomes. Contributing to the current debate around building civic universities and reframing the concept of civility systemically, I propose reconfiguring management education around four different principles: generalized reciprocity, substantive rationality, diverse organizing, and a system approach. I suggest that these are the pedagogical foundations for civic management education capable of producing cooperative humans, substantive business schools, fairer societies, and thriving ecosystems.
Ecological and climate crises are threatening human survival. Our generation is already suffering from the upheavals these issues cause, and their catastrophic consequences are there for all to see: intense droughts and floods, severe fires and water scarcity, melting polar ice, and biodiversity loss, among others. This is happening right now and will worsen in the years ahead ([IPCC, 2021](#page-14-0);[ Ripple, Wolf, News](#page-16-0)[ome, Barnard, & Moomaw, 2020)](#page-16-0). The effects of human-caused environmental degradation are "irreversible on the timescale of people alive today" ([NASA, n.d.](#page-15-0)), but if previous generations have failed in protecting our common future, we still have an opportunity to mitigate the suffering of generations to come and that of other species. A challenge of this kind requires major changes to the way we manage our collective home. It calls for cooperation, longsightedness, and critical, creative, and system thinking. Educational institutions, including universities,

Yet, despite many declaring an ecological and climate emergency, universities across the world are far from being inspiring agents of change. On the contrary, contemporary higher education has been described as a place where environmental and social challenges are exacerbated, defined as "whackademia" [(Hill, 2012)](#page-14-0), "lower-ed" [(Cottom, 2017](#page-13-0)), a "wrecked" institution [(Newfield, 2018](#page-15-0)), a "zombie" ([Murphy, 2017](#page-15-0)), and a "ghost" university [(Fleming, 2021b](#page-13-0)). In such a desolate scenario, meet the contemporary business school: a place where competition, self-interest, greed, and short-termism are not only accepted but also normalized and extensively recreated [(Khurana, 2007](#page-15-0);[ Parker,](#page-16-0) [2018](#page-16-0);[Wang, Malhotra, & Murnighan, 2011](#page-16-0)).
Management scholars have long exposed the inadequacy of management education in addressing the wicked problems confronting business and society. Critiques have included nostalgic assessments, yearning for a time when the business school was a cradle of professionalism and morality for a management elite [(Augier & March, 2011;](#page-12-0)[ Khurana, 2007;](#page-15-0) O'[Connor, 2012)](#page-15-0); reformist appraisals, advocating for
a more sustainable, responsible, or plural business school [(Ghoshal, 2005;](#page-14-0)[ Podolny, 2009](#page-16-0)); and transformative appeals [(Contu, 2009](#page-13-0);[ Cunliffe, Forray, &](#page-13-0) [Knights, 2002;](#page-13-0)[ Grey, 2004)](#page-14-0) calling in the "bulldozers" ([Parker, 2018](#page-16-0)). However, this discussion has resulted in very little change. As[ Fleming (2021b)](#page-13-0) noted: "No matter how much vitriol academics direct at the neoliberal university, none of it seems to make a difference." Thus, the temptation is strong to surrender to cynicism and believe that change is unattainable or "nearly impossible" [(Fleming, 2021b](#page-13-0): 18).
One reason why change has been difficult to achieve is that contemporary approaches to higher education including management education—have been supported by a policy framework designed to protect and enhance the status quo [(Angus, 2015](#page-12-0);[ Lockford,](#page-15-0) [2017](#page-15-0);[ Maisuria, 2014](#page-15-0)). That agenda, defined as "neoliberalism," includes policies in support of a "free" market, minimal government intervention, competition, and privatization ([Maisuria & Cole,](#page-15-0) [2017](#page-15-0)). First put into practice by the Chilean dictatorship in the 1970s, neoliberalism became the flagship policy framework of the British and U.S. governments in subsequent years, and a dominant approach to the political economy worldwide ([Maisuria, 2014](#page-15-0)). During the last three decades, neoliberalism has entered higher education, becoming normalized and an "almost natural" condition ([Mai](#page-15-0)[suria & Cole, 2017](#page-15-0): 605). The neoliberal university has been described as an "edu-factory," in which students are customers who must be satisfied at all costs ([Fleming, 2020](#page-13-0): 1307); an institution underpinned by "an ethic of efficiency and productivity" [(Vassallo,](#page-16-0) [2013:](#page-16-0) 570), in which competition—rather than cooperation—is encouraged and enhanced at every level [(Kallio, Kallio, Tienari, & Hyvonen, 2016)](#page-14-0); and a € commodity governed by market forces and "business opportunities" that "determine its potential for survival" [(Maisuria & Cole, 2017:](#page-15-0) 607). Transforming management education will therefore necessarily require understanding, critiquing, and redefining "common sense" (appreciating that common sense is constituted by learnt behaviors [see[ Haidt, 2008;](#page-14-0) [Solomon, 1993]](#page-16-0)), as well as changing the policy framework that supports it.
This essay has three objectives. First, to lay bare the implicit assumptions that drive contemporary management education by highlighting the dysfunctional consequences they produce on the system. Second, to propose an alternative approach (i.e. a civic management education [CME]) by underlining its functions. Third, to advance strategies for change. By "dysfunctions," I mean the regular consequences
that harm the "organism"—that is, the system in which dysfunctions are situated; by "functions," I imply the "regular consequences that benefit the organism" ([Keltner & Gross, 1999:](#page-14-0) 469), and by "system" the wider set of interdependent relationships tying business and society to the natural environment [(Capra, 1982](#page-13-0)) (for a more detailed account of these concepts, see[ Cohen, 1982;](#page-13-0)[ Lindebaum, 2017](#page-15-0)).
In the first section, titled "On civility," before unpacking the process through which contemporary management education yields dysfunctional outcomes, and before exploring CME's functions and implementation strategies, I clarify the essay's approach to civility.
In the second section, titled "Dysfunctional consequences of neoliberal management education," I focus on the current state of affairs. Starting from the individual level and progressively "zooming out" to the institutional, societal, and environmental context, I identify four harmful, yet often unintended, consequences of contemporary management education. They include, respectively, the normalization and reproduction of greed, the creation of instrumental business schools, the exacerbation of inequality, and ecosystem degradation. I highlight that such dysfunctional consequences are supported by four fundamental assumptions with deep historical roots, which have become normalized and part of the dominant common sense. They are: self-interest, instrumental rationality, capitalist organizing, and a mechanistic approach to management. As I will explain further below, these assumptions generate self-fulfilling prophecies [(Merton, 1948](#page-15-0)).
In the third section, titled "Functions of civic management education," I propose redefining management education following four principles: generalized reciprocity, substantive rationality, diverse organizing, and a system approach to management. I suggest that these are the pedagogical foundations for CME. To the extent that the four assumptions considered in the second section produce dysfunctions, these four principles can produce regular positive consequences that enable long-lasting economic, social, and ecological prosperity, including the nourishment of cooperative humans, substantive business schools, income and wealth distribution, and ecosystem regeneration.
The fourth section, titled "Doing civic management education," is a call for action, exploring how CME can be realized in practice.
# ON CIVILITY
This essay proposes to reconfigure management education around the concept of civility, considered
as the pursuit of ecological flourishing, inclusive of human flourishing. This understanding allows moving beyond narrow and anthropocentric approaches to civility.
Civility has recently entered university boardrooms in the United Kingdom following the constitution, in 2018, of the Civic University Commission, and, in 2019, of the Civic University Network. In this context, civility is mainly understood in terms of civic engagement—that is, partnerships that tie universities to their local communities to "build mutually beneficial relationships for the public good" ([Civic University Network, n.d.)](#page-13-0), with an eye to widening access to higher education. Therefore, the debate around the civic university has focused on community engagement [(Brink, 2018:](#page-13-0) 285–334) and socially engaged research ([Goodard, 2009)](#page-14-0). However, despite placing civility in the spotlight, this conversation has hardly been transformative: while advocating for a more engaged pedagogy, it has not yet thoroughly questioned the basic principles grounding the neoliberal university.
A more transformative notion of civility is that of civil economy, a historic Italian approach to economics, drawing upon the Aristotelian Nicomachean Ethics [(Aristotle, 350 BCE/2002](#page-12-0)), and describing the nature of business as essentially relational and focused on the goal of fulfilling public happiness ([Bruni & Zamagni, 2007](#page-13-0)). Civil economy emerged in Italy in the first half of the 15th century, during the first phase of the Italian renaissance, as an expression of the civic humanism of the time [(Bracciolini,](#page-13-0) [1429/1994](#page-13-0);[ Palmieri, 1440/1981](#page-15-0)), and flourished in the second half of the 18th century, during the Italian enlightenment [(Filangeri, 1780/2003; Geno](#page-13-0)[vesi, 1757](#page-13-0)–1758;[ Verri, 1763/1963)](#page-16-0). Although this approach to civility is more transformative, it is again insufficient to break the self-fulfilling prophecies inherent in contemporary management education as it is largely locked into anthropocentric narratives. Indeed, civil economy mostly considers the environment as a subject absorbed in the social dimension of human relations (e.g., civic virtues as inclusive of ecological virtues) and does not consider ecological relationships as a matter of explicit concern. This approach has impacted third-sector understandings internationally. For example, nature is a missing theme in the seven cooperative principles of the International Cooperative Alliance, implicitly considered within the "Concern for community" [(ICA, n.d.)](#page-14-0).
This essay calls for a new paradigmatic orientation to civility. Combining virtue ethics with environmental ethics [(Hursthouse, 2007](#page-14-0);[ Kawall, 2017;](#page-14-0)
[Sandler, 2016](#page-16-0)), I suggest emphasizing ecological virtues as inclusive of civic virtues, acknowledging the interdependent relationships between the environment, society, and business [(Ergene, Banerjee, &](#page-13-0) [Hoffman, 2021)](#page-13-0); and redefining civility as the pursuit of ecological flourishing, inclusive of human flourishing ([Sandler, 2016](#page-16-0)). This approach to civility, defined in terms of "civic management education," serves as an antidote to neoliberalism: to the neoliberal university's competitive doctrine, CME counterposes a cooperative ethos; while the "Neoliberal U" leads to "an increasingly neoliberal you" ([Ashcraft, 2017:](#page-12-0) 37), CME empowers students to exercise critical thinking and self-realization, in the context of a relational and civic life; and while neoliberal management education leads to the exacerbation of inequality and ecological degradation ([Fotaki & Prasad, 2015](#page-13-0);[ Gladwin, 1993](#page-14-0)), CME promotes social and environmental justice. Framing change in terms of civility helps build momentum around a concept that has already entered the public debate, at a time when it is being rediscovered in higher education, while at the same time building and growing a network of like-minded scholars across different disciplines and beyond the academic community. To support worldwide transitions, CME needs to put at the heart of management education multiple philosophies based on the pursuit of ecological flourishing (e.g., those developed around the concepts of buen vivir [good living] and ubuntu [humaneness]) ([Naude, 2019; Ordo](#page-15-0)nez, ~ [Shannon, & d](#page-15-0)'Auria, 2022). While this essay identifies one possible way out of the neoliberal drift in higher education, it is important to remark that "What is the alternative?" must remain a question with multiple, situated, and localized answers ([Parker, Cheney, Fournier, & Land, 2014](#page-16-0)).
## DYSFUNCTIONAL CONSEQUENCES OF NEOLIBERAL MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
According to[ Merton (1968:](#page-15-0) 94), dysfunctional consequences are precursors to change.
When the net balance of the aggregate of consequences of an existing social structure is clearly dysfunctional, there develops a strong and insistent pressure for change. It is possible… that beyond a given point, this pressure will inevitably result in more or less predetermined directions of social change.
In this section, I will focus on the dysfunctional consequences of contemporary (neoliberal) management education and uncover the preconceptions generating them. Change is needed to break the
vicious cycles creating greedy individuals, instrumental business schools, inequality, and ecosystem degradation. Ultimately, change is needed to survive as a species.
## Greedy Individuals
Contemporary management education produces serious, albeit unintended, consequences on our character, on who we are as human beings. In a study published in 2011, Wang and colleagues demonstrated how economics education in business schools is consistently associated with a positive perception of greed generally, a positive attitude toward one's greedy actions, and reduced sensibility toward the impact of such action on others ([Wang](#page-16-0) [et al., 2011)](#page-16-0). Because the business school teaches students that economic agents operate in a hostile environment of ruthless competition, students expect nothing less and behave accordingly. The relationship between business education and greed was further examined by[ Walker (1992).](#page-16-0) Her study showed how MBA education is constructed upon the premise that: "1) people are self-interested utilitymaximizers, 2) individuals should be unimpeded in the pursuit of their own self-interest through 'economic' transactions, and 3) virtually all human interactions are economic transactions" ([Walker,](#page-16-0) [1992](#page-16-0): 273). These preconceptions of human nature affect teaching in different disciplines beyond economics and management (e.g., finance education narrowly focusing on maximizing returns in the shortest period) and are institutionally reinforced (e.g., through reward systems designed around competition, the assessment of individual performance and the overuse of monetary prizes).
The anthropological assumption that humans are consistently motivated by self-interest emerged in Europe after the Renaissance, with the beginning of the modern age. First[ Machiavelli (1532/2014)](#page-15-0) and then[ Hobbes (1651)](#page-14-0) depicted the human condition as one of fear, wickedness, and incivility, characterized by violent competition and the never-ending struggle to overpower fellow men. That was the result of a very particular historical time, which saw Europe put to fire and sword by ferocious religious wars. The essential vision of Hobbes is that a human is a wolf to other humans (homo homini lupus). Hence the need to be subjected to a powerful authority (a Prince for[ Machiavelli [1532/2014]](#page-15-0), a Leviathan for[ Hobbes [1651](#page-14-0)]) to limit humans' inner propensity for violence. In essence, according to[ Hobbes (1651:](#page-14-0) 7), humans are self-interested by nature: "We do not
[…] by nature seek Society for its own sake, but that we may receive some Honor or Profit from it." The understanding of human nature as self-interested shaped the mathematical models forming the basis of late-19th- and early-20th-century neoclassical economics ([Jevons, 1865;](#page-14-0)[ Pareto, 1920](#page-16-0);[ Robbins,](#page-16-0) [1932](#page-16-0)), which still hold center stage in contemporary management education.
If the direct result of understanding human nature as self-interested is greedy individuals, the indirect consequences of this preconception are much wider, and are harmful for the environment, society, and business itself. Take business, for example. The dysfunctions generated by greed have been in the public eye for decades but were brought into stark relief during the global financial crisis of 2007–2008. Businesses led by profit-driven, myopic CEOs experienced greater losses in the short-run and took longer to recover from the crisis ([Sajko, Boone, & Buyl,](#page-16-0) [2020](#page-16-0)). Greed is not well-received by customers either. Indeed, perceived corporate greed leads to adverse consumer reactions ([Lim, 2020](#page-15-0)) and negative attitudes toward business [(Caruana, Vella,](#page-13-0) [Konietzny, & Chircop, 2018](#page-13-0)). In a vicious cycle, definitions of human nature as self-interested generate greedy individuals [(Wang et al., 2011)](#page-16-0); greed validates assumptions of self-interest, which worsen greed itself, and so on.[ Merton (1948](#page-15-0): 194) explained this dynamic as a "self-fulfilling prophecy":
Men respond not only to the objective features of a situation, but also, and at times primarily, to the meaning this situation has for them. And once they have assigned some meaning to the situation, their consequent behavior and some of the consequences of that behavior are determined by the ascribed meaning.
In short, by teaching self-interest maximization the business school produces greedy individuals.
## Instrumental Business Schools
Contemporary business education produces dysfunctional institutional consequences.[ Kitchener](#page-15-0) [and Delbridge (2020)](#page-15-0) argued that management learning and teaching are pervaded by instrumental rationality, and illustrated the impacts this has on institutional expectations (e.g., excessive preoccupation with outputs, performance indicators and rankings). Governed through competitive dynamics and stimulated by the possibility to climb hierarchies and league tables, the business school systematically fails to care about those who care, narrowly focused as it is on producing outputs to achieve high levels of performance, measured through research outputs,
journal rankings, employability rates, etc.[ Weber](#page-16-0) [(1922/1978](#page-16-0): 24) defined instrumental rationality as output-oriented action, mainly concerned with "the attainment of the actor's own rationally pursued and calculated ends." Furthermore,[ Horkheimer (1974:](#page-14-0) 3–4) explained that this type of rationality focuses on "gain or advantage," and is essentially concerned with "the adequacy of procedure for purposes more or less taken for granted and supposedly selfexplanatory," without questioning "whether the purposes as such are reasonable." This instrumental approach is built through institutions designed to be hierarchical and competitive—that is, governed though "publish or perish" and "up or out" dynamics—and strengthened by policy frameworks that support neoliberal norms and values [(Angus,](#page-12-0) [2015](#page-12-0)).
Excessive instrumentality in business schools produces several serious consequences—for example, on the nature and purpose of academia, on the mental health and well-being of those who inhabit it, and on the future of work. First, a narrow focus on instrumental rationality transforms the nature and purpose of higher education from a public and common good that encourages scholars to exercise critical judgement, advance human knowledge, and engage with the grand challenges of our time, to a private good that encourages buyers to pursue individual benefits and private economic aspirations ([Busch, 2017;](#page-13-0) [Shapiro, 2005; van Houtum & van Uden, 2022](#page-16-0)). As [Podolny (2009)](#page-16-0) explained, contemporary business schools encourage students to ask not "How do I want to change the world for the better?" but "What can I do to make the most money?" From a research point of view, instrumental rationality leads to what [Tourish (2020:](#page-16-0) 99) defined as "The triumph of nonsense in management studies," with particular reference to the excessive concern of academics with research outputs to increase their h-index rather than on meaningful research to make a positive contribution to society [(McKiernan & Tsui, 2019](#page-15-0)).
Second, strong pressures to perform, combined with the neoliberalization and itemization of academic labor, have a dramatic impact on the mental health of both students and academic staff. In his recent book Dark Academia. How Universities Die [Fleming (2021a)](#page-13-0) denounced these dysfunctional dynamics as literally killing the university. In 2018, the rates of depression and anxiety among postgraduate students worldwide were estimated to be six times higher than those in the general population ([Evans, Bira, Gastelum, Weiss, & Vanderford, 2018)](#page-13-0). In 2020, a survey of over 1,000 U.S. faculty members
showed that the pandemic dramatically exacerbated the already high levels of stress in academia, with almost 70% of respondents reporting that they feel under pressure ([Gewin, 2021](#page-14-0)), and with consequent rampant burnout and other serious medical conditions. A closer look at the business school reveals that its culture of competition, combined with performance pressures and high workload demands, further deteriorates the mental health of students and staff, leading to a particularly severe mental health crisis [(Edwards, Martin, & Ashkanasy, 2021;](#page-13-0) [Harley, 2019](#page-14-0)). What is the real cost of learning and teaching in higher education today? Is it worth it?
Third, as the business school is transformed into an instrumental institution, emptied of its civic purpose, the importance of management education to equip human agents with the ability to formulate complex judgements wanes too. Therefore, because of the inherent complexity and paradoxical nature of management being overlooked [(Smith & Lewis,](#page-16-0) [2011](#page-16-0)), management practice and education become mere rule-following activities, and human judgment in decision-making becomes potentially replaceable by artificially intelligent algorithms ([Moser, den](#page-15-0) [Hond, & Lindebaum, 2022)](#page-15-0). A colleague recently lamented: "Our students see us as a human Alexa, which perhaps explains why we experience often direct, sometimes curt exchanges with them. 'Alexa, how do I get a first?'" A second vicious cycle is completed: definitions of human rationality as purely instrumental produce instrumentally rational institutions ([Kitchener & Delbridge, 2020](#page-15-0)), which in turn validate instrumental rationality and aggravate its detrimental consequences.
### Inequality
Contemporary approaches to management education produce dysfunctional societal consequences. An example of such damage is the (re)production of socioeconomic inequalities, exacerbated by teaching capitalism dogmatically and uncritically.[ Parker](#page-16-0) [(2018)](#page-16-0) highlighted that most business schools teach capitalism as "the only alternative" worth serious consideration. While wage employment, capital accumulation, and competition between firms are unquestioned pillars of management education, ideas such as cooperative ownership, social entrepreneurship, and democratic planning are either ignored altogether or confined to the margins of business and management curricula [(Adler, Forbes &](#page-12-0) [Willmott, 2007](#page-12-0);[ Parker et al., 2014](#page-16-0)). In this context, [Fotaki and Prasad (2015)](#page-13-0) illuminated not only how
capitalism dominates the business school curricula but how capitalist organizing is taught uncritically that is, without problematizing the assumptions upon which it resides and the dysfunctional consequences it produces. Indeed, they argued that business schools have systematically avoided critically engaging with "how businesses are implicated in the generation and maintenance of economic inequality, and also how they are affected by its negative consequences" ([Fotaki & Prasad, 2015](#page-13-0): 557). Management research has been paying increasing attention to the relationship between management education and socioeconomic inequality [(Kumar et al., 2022)](#page-15-0). This is an important conversation to hold, considering that the business school itself is a direct representation of inequality. In North America, the tuition fees for a two-year MBA at a top business school (e.g., Harvard Business School, Stanford Graduate School of Business, The Wharton School, etc.) are over $140,000. In Europe, a one-year MBA at a prestigious institution can cost over $90,000 (e.g., at the London Business School in the United Kingdom; INSEAD in France, or IESE in Spain). The same goes for other top-ranked business schools all over the world (e.g., in Asia, a two-year MBA at the Indian Institute of Management in Bangalore can cost over $40,000). The consequence of this is not only a business school that clearly does not represent society, but also creates an extremely unrepresentative corporate sector, which often hires from these institutions. It is sufficient to take a look at the list of MBA graduates who are chief executives of a Financial Times 500—the world's largest companies by market capitalization—to realize that the senior management of global corporations are a boys' club [(Palin &](#page-15-0) [Bernard, 2015)](#page-15-0).
The latest World Inequality Report [(Chancel,](#page-13-0) [Piketty, Saez, & Zucman, 2022)](#page-13-0) showed that, since the 1980s, income and wealth inequality have dramatically increased globally. While the poorest half of the global population currently earns 8.5% of the global income and possesses only 2% of the global wealth, the richest 10% takes 52% of all income and owns 76% of all wealth [(Chancel et al., 2022)](#page-13-0). Economic inequality is closely tied to gender inequality (e.g., women's share of labor income stands at less than 35%) and environmental inequality (e.g., the top 10% of carbon emitters globally produce close to 50% of total emissions, while the bottom 50% are only responsible for 12% of the total) ([Chancel et al.,](#page-13-0) [2022](#page-13-0)). It is well-established that economic inequality is a feature of capitalism ([Piketty, 2014)](#page-16-0), and that it is exacerbated by myopic approaches to business that
are narrowly concerned with profit-maximization ([Fotaki & Prasad, 2015)](#page-13-0). It is also clear that inequality is detrimental to society and to business itself, causing social, political, and economic instability ([Bapuji, 2015](#page-12-0);[ Stiglitz, 2012; United Nations, 2020](#page-16-0)). In addition, accounting measures such as the "ecological footprint" have shown how the ecological space on Earth is not shared equally, with high-income countries responsible for using a disproportionate amount of natural resources versus lower-income countries, and consuming them at a much faster rate than the planet can regenerate ([NFA, 2021)](#page-15-0). Yet, instead of exposing the systematic harm that neoliberal business models produce on the environment, society, and business, management education either ignores these dysfunctions or relegates them to a handful of exceptional cases of bad management practices (e.g., scandals such as Enron and Volkswagen) or extraordinary critical circumstances (e.g., the bailout of American International Group in the aftermath of the global financial crisis) ([Fotaki & Prasad, 2015](#page-13-0)). Instead of critiquing the colonial nature of our industrial system and the drain the Global North has imposed—and continues to impose—on the Global South, business education still relies on—and teaches—colonial, extractive, and linear systems of production [(Hickel, Sullivan, &](#page-14-0) [Zoomkawala, 2021](#page-14-0)). Herein lies the source of a third vicious cycle, which is closely connected to the previous two: teaching capitalism uncritically exacerbates its dysfunctional societal consequences while reinforcing understandings of capitalism as "the only alternative" [(Parker, 2018](#page-16-0)), which in turn worsen the harm to society while maintaining narrow-mindedness and related issues.
### Ecosystem Degradation
Current approaches to management education have dysfunctional consequences on the ecological system in which society, institutions, and individuals exist. Clearly, business schools have an impact on the environment, related to procurement practices, infrastructure efficiency, choices of transport, and so forth. For example,[ Gill (2021)](#page-14-0) pointed out the consequences on climate change of the unfettered use of long-haul flights regularly taken by academics to attend conferences, conduct research, or undertake teaching and other activities. The good news is that efforts have been made to lower the carbon footprint of business schools, especially since the COVID-19 pandemic and the climate emergency declarations of many universities, followed by
institutional commitments to pursue various routes to carbon "net-zero." However, beyond the direct impact of business schools on the environment lie deeper and indirect dysfunctional consequences, which originate from understandings of management as a mechanistic discipline. The bad news is that these dynamics largely remain unquestioned.
The first economic rule taught to a first-year undergraduate student is the economic equilibrium determined by the supply and demand curves, "describing the economy as if it were a stable, mechanical system" ([Raworth, 2017](#page-16-0): 129). The mechanistic approach to management considers the economy, society, and the environment as cogs of a machine that can be pulled apart and studied, understood, and managed separately. Their interconnections may be acknowledged in the curriculum (e.g., though introducing corporate social responsibility and triple bottom line theories), but their interdependence, dynamicity, and complexity are largely ignored. Business and management theory is mostly taught as if ecology, politics, and economics were separate [(Green, 2013](#page-14-0)). Indeed, it is rare to find ecological degradation, environmental justice, climate change, and other planetary boundaries within a business curriculum ([Molthan-Hill, Worsfold, Nagy,](#page-15-0) [Leal Filho, & Mifsud, 2019](#page-15-0)). In the business school, the relationship between business and nature when considered in the first place—is largely explained through environmental economics, a branch of neoclassical economics that emerged in the 1970s with the aim of attributing a monetary value to natural resources, which considers the environment as a "missing market" and environmental degradation as a "market failure" [(Turner, Pearce, & Bateman,](#page-16-0) [1994](#page-16-0)). Environmental economics holds blind faith in the market as a useful allocation mechanism able to safeguard nature, and in economic growth as the way forward to improve the quality of the environment (e.g., following the Kuznets curve, as explained by[ Grossman and Krueger [1995](#page-14-0)]). In the context of environmental economics, ecological degradation is considered an "externality" to the economy activity—that is, "external" insofar that business theory does not account for it.
As early as 1993, management academics came to a "disturbing and terrifying" realization: far from increasing awareness of the interdependence between the environment, society, and business, management education unintentionally upholds eco-illiteracy ([Gladwin, 1993:](#page-14-0) 110). Not only are eco-illiterate graduates ill-equipped to navigate the grand challenges of our time, but this ignorance aggravates the
ecosystem degradation caused by reckless business practices. Indeed, instead of including ecological thinking in the curriculum (e.g.,[ Banerjee & Arjali](#page-12-0)es, [2021](#page-12-0);[ Capra, 1982](#page-13-0);[ Raworth, 2017; Savory, 1999](#page-16-0)), management education promotes "a wide array of theories, doctrines, models, and analytical methods that… serve to directly or indirectly harm the biosphere" [(Gladwin, 1993](#page-14-0): 111). The fourth vicious cycle is accomplished: mechanistic approaches to management education produce eco-illiteracy, which intensifies ecosystem degradation while strengthening silo thinking, which aggravates the ecological crises while maintaining ignorance, and so on. Ultimately, the dysfunctional consequences of contemporary management education are threatening human survival.
## FUNCTIONS OF CIVIC MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
How can the tragic, vicious cycle of self-fulfilling prophecies be broken?[ Merton (1948:](#page-15-0) 197) suggested that:
The initial definition of the situation which has set the circle in motion must be abandoned. Only when the original assumption is questioned and a new definition of the situation introduced, does the consequent flow of events give the lie to the assumption. Only then does the belief no longer father the reality.
To break the self-fulfilling prophecies causing systemic harm, management education needs to be shaken at its very foundations. In this section, I will redefine the key assumptions driving the contemporary business school, highlighting the regular consequences that adopting CME will have for individuals, institutions, societies, and ecosystems.
### Cooperative Humans
The first step is to redefine human nature as cooperative—characterized by a sense of responsibility to others. This understanding constitutes the historical foundations of civil economy, which reverses Hobbes's adage, arguing that homo homini natura amicus est (literally: that a human is a friend to other humans by nature) (as cited in[ Bruni, 2012](#page-13-0)) and considers humans as "civil animals" [(Garin, 1952/](#page-13-0) [1994:](#page-13-0) 54). Anthropologists and historians have discussed issues of human nature ever since the dawn of civilization (for "a hopeful history," see[ Bregman,](#page-13-0) [2020)](#page-13-0). Evidence of social behavior has been identified in Neanderthals: patterns of healed trauma (e.g., survival after major injuries and recovery from severe
impairments) suggest that our ancient human relatives used to live in groups, practice mutual care, and be invested in each other's well-being [(Spikins,](#page-16-0) [Needham, Tilley, & Hitchens,](#page-16-0) 2018). A story attributed to the anthropologist Margaret Mead tells of a student once asking her what she regarded to be the first sign of human civilization. The inquirer was expecting an answer involving the production of some sort of output, such as stone tools, clay pots, or cave paintings. However, Mead allegedly replied: "A healed human femur" [(Brand & Yancey, 1980:](#page-13-0) 68). It was not artifacts crafted by primitive human beings, but the commitment to mutual support. Civilization could proceed because of the capacity to cooperate and care for one another.
Now, 15,000 years later, the same cooperative skills could help us navigate the grand challenges of our time. However, for that to happen, the concept of "other" needs to be extended beyond our fellow humans, to include the ecological system in which our species is embedded. Yet, reciprocity—considered by civil economists as the most important social norm for the civic life—is usually described as a form of exchange between social agents only [(Bruni &](#page-13-0) [Zamagni, 2009)](#page-13-0). Reciprocity-based exchanges are defined as independent (i.e., each connection is determined by a willingness to give that is untied to previous exchanges), bidirectional (i.e., each connection implies responsiveness), and transitive (i.e., the response can be directed toward the giver or another person) [(Kolm, 1994](#page-15-0);[ Zamagni, 2007](#page-16-0)). Consider, for example, that A, B, and C are neighbors. B and C are self-isolating, having tested positive with COVID-19. A makes soup and leaves some on B's doorstep. A few days later, B does the same for C, when they are in need of help, and shares some with A too.
When extending the concept of "other" beyond our own kind—for instance, at ecosystem scale and beyond our own time—for example, future generations—reciprocity is "generalized" [(Osti, 1999)](#page-15-0). Consider again, for example, that A volunteers at a neighborhood community garden, where they source the ingredients for the soup. Growing organically, A contributes to caring for the soil (D) and for wildlife (E). Healthy soil and thriving insect populations (e.g., pollinators) ensure a bountiful crop, which is able to feed A, B, and C at once, while also preserving a flourishing ecosystem for future generations of community gardeners (F). Generalized reciprocity considers exchange as an interconnected web of relationships. It allows thinking in terms of systems, acknowledging the interdependence between human beings and nature.
There is clear evidence that assuming humans are self-interested produces dysfunctions that harm the system (e.g., it enhances greed, as demonstrated by [Wang et al. [2011]](#page-16-0)). Similarly, understanding human nature as cooperative can produce regular consequences that enable the system to thrive. Researching self-fulfilling prophecies in the classroom,[ Rosenthal](#page-16-0) [and Jacobson (1968)](#page-16-0) discovered that expectations do influence behavior both positively and negatively: students assumed to be high-achieving perform better than those assumed to be low-achieving. This is what the authors defined as the "Pygmalion effect." It seems reasonable, then, to suggest that assuming students are cooperative will nourish their potential to cooperate.[ Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968)](#page-16-0)—and many other academics after them (e.g.,[ Chen &](#page-13-0) [Klimosk, 2003; Eden, 1992; Farrukh, Meng & Raza,](#page-13-0) [2022](#page-13-0))—demonstrated empirically that students tend to conform to the image others have of them: expecting they are self-interested and utility-maximizers actively encourages greedy behavior ([Wang et al.,](#page-16-0) [2011](#page-16-0)); likewise, expecting they are intrinsically reciprocal nourishes cooperation. A few months ago, I went hiking in the mountains near my home. I had just started a long ascent when I met a fellow hiker. He had paused by the side of the path, busy attaching a few sticks to his already heavy rucksack. I asked what he was up to. He said: "I'm taking some wood up to the highest refuge, this is what people do here. There are no trees up there. Somebody will need wood to light a fire one day." In future, on the way up, I will always carry a couple of sticks (and on the way down, some litter that the wind or other hikers leave behind). This is how the first vicious cycle can be broken: expect self-interest, create greed ([Wang](#page-16-0) [et al., 2011](#page-16-0)); expect reciprocity, create cooperation.
### Substantive Business Schools
Understandings of human nature as cooperative lay the foundation for a different kind of business school: an institution grounded in substantive rationality, a school with a civic purpose.[ Weber,](#page-16-0) [(1922/1978:](#page-16-0) 24) defined substantive rationality as value-oriented action "determined by a conscious belief in the value for its own sake of some [ … ] behavior, independently of its prospects of success." [Habermas (1979](#page-14-0): 84–85) further illuminated this type of rationality, which he called "communicative rationality," considering that "the development of students' preparedness to make value judgements about the world" should be an important concern for education (see also
[Gibson, 2011](#page-14-0): 713). A value-oriented business school is one that nourishes critical thinking: a place that "bring[s] values into the classroom for analysis and discussion" ([Grey, 2004](#page-14-0)).
Different types of rationality are needed to understand, critique, and transform social realities [(Kalberg,](#page-14-0) [1980)](#page-14-0). Introducing the theory and practice of substantive rationality in business schools can generate several beneficial consequences—for example, building civic engagement, restoring a fulfilling academic life, and enhancing humane work. First, exercising the ability to make value judgments empowers students to participate actively and responsibly to the management of our collective home, rediscovering the very meaning of the word "education." From the Latin educere —to lead (ducere) out (ex), education is a process of empowerment, directed toward unfolding the powers of individuals as members of a community. In the words of[ Freire (1970](#page-13-0): 15):
Education either functions as an instrument which is used to facilitate integration of the younger generation into the logic of the present system and bring about conformity or it becomes the practice of freedom, the means by which men and women deal critically and creatively with reality and discover how to participate in the transformation of their world.
Reframing education as civic engagement is the first step toward "commoning" the business school ([Locatelli, 2018; Noble & Ross, 2019](#page-15-0))—that is, developing cooperative approaches to educational governance that empower business school's members to participate in decision making [(Hursh, 2016](#page-14-0)).
Second, while a narrow focus on instrumental rationality sucks the life out of students and staff ([Fleming, 2020](#page-13-0),[ 2021a, 2021b)](#page-13-0), balancing instrumental and substantive rationality restores meaningful work in academia, replenishing a sense of purpose and fulfillment. As[ Tourish (2020](#page-16-0): 107) suggested:
I can think of no better purpose than addressing the grand challenges that confront our species, and which at present we mostly ignore… [we must do that] for our own sakes and more importantly for the benefit of the societies in which we live.
This is also in line with the desire by "Generation Z" to have jobs that are not only profitable but also, most importantly, personally fulfilling and civicminded ([NSHSS, 2018](#page-15-0)).
Third, while the future of work seems inevitably tied to artificial intelligence (AI)—and many jobs are being replaced by the calculative ability of ever more intelligent algorithms—AI will never [(Smith, 2019)](#page-16-0), or should never [(Moser et al., 2022)](#page-15-0), fully substitute
human judgment in decision-making. Therefore, designing the business school around different forms of rationality is a way to "remain adaptive in the socio-technological world that we now inhabit" and to reduce the risk of losing control over artificially intelligent technology [(Moser et al., 2022:](#page-15-0) 140).
Adopting a system perspective to substantive rationality means bringing ecological values and virtues into the classroom (e.g., care for nature, environmental justice, frugality, etc.) and redefine public happiness as a long-term ecological flourishing that includes, but without being restricted to, human flourishing. A system approach also helps to frame employment as "right livelihood"—that is, the idea that students should be supported to pursue "an honest occupation," one that acknowledges one's survival is connected with that of others, promotes awareness of the consequences that one's actions have on other people and the natural world, and thereafter encourages acting responsibly ([The Right](#page-16-0) [Livelihood Award, n.d.](#page-16-0)). Another vicious cycle can hence be broken—sow instrumentality, harvest instrumentally rational institutions; sow critical and systemic thinking, harvest civic business schools.
## Income and Wealth Distribution
When latent assumptions in management education are exposed and appropriately questioned, the role of neoliberal capitalism in exacerbating economic, social, and environmental inequality can no longer be ignored ([Fotaki & Prasad, 2015](#page-13-0)). A substantially rational business school provides a fertile ground for questioning taken-for-granted assumptions and seemingly inevitable consequences, including challenging the preconception that "there is no alternative" to neoliberal capitalism. Research on alternative organization [(Berti & Pitelis, 2022;](#page-12-0) [Gibson-Graham et al., 2013](#page-14-0);[ Parker et al., 2014)](#page-16-0) has demystified the assumption that capitalist enterprise is the only—or necessarily most effective, or even most efficient—way of organizing. For instance,[ Berti](#page-12-0) [and Pitelis (2022)](#page-12-0) have shown how hybrid firms can possess comparative efficiency advantages to both capitalist and cooperative organizations, proving to be more efficient—as well as fairer—than traditional capitalist firms. Multistakeholder organizations such as cooperatives and social enterprises can also align multiple interests across a wide range of interested parties, distributing both income (e.g., salary) and wealth (e.g., ownership and democratic control of the organization) [(Tortia & Borzaga, 2020)](#page-16-0).
Embracing a pluralistic view of economics (i.e., ensuring that alternative organizations have a prominent space in business studies) does not mean replacing one system of domination with another (e.g., it should not erase neoclassical economics from the curriculum), but entails exposing students to different ways of thinking and organizing—for example, to study the "scientific management" of Ford alongside the "cooperative management" of Suma Foods ([Parker, 2018:](#page-16-0) 119), analyzing, critiquing, and considering both in light of their context. When opening up the discipline of management to include a diverse range of approaches, it is possible to stop considering it in a restrictive sense, as a practice that necessarily relies on hierarchy, inequality of status and reward, information asymmetry, externalization of costs, appropriation through unequal exchange, and exponential economic growth. In other words, it is possible to recognize that inequality is not inevitable nor necessary: it is a design choice or, in[ Raworth](#page-16-0)'s [(2017](#page-16-0): 29) words, "a design failure." Organizations can be designed to be distributive of the value they generate—including distributing wealth (e.g., originating from controlling natural resources, business, technology, etc.). Encouraging students to work together to develop distributive solutions, with the support of their teachers and the mediation of the communities they inhabit, can help produce longlasting economic, social, and ecological prosperity, including reducing inequality. According to[ Raw](#page-16-0)[orth (2017)](#page-16-0), to reduce inequality, the economy needs to be structured as a "distributed network," inspired by ecosystems' designs, where balance—rather than growth—is the driving force.
I will always remember what happened when a business and management student joined our social economy cohort to catch up on a lecture he had missed. The professor gave the same lecture on game theory to the two cohorts, which differed substantially: business and management students had been indoctrinated with neoclassical economics for two years, while social economy students were used to considering business in the context of a diverse economy. We played the "ultimatum game": the professor asked us to imagine there were 100 one-euro coins on the table, to be shared between ourselves and another person; she asked us to make a sharing proposal, indicating how many coins we wanted to take and how many to give. The other could then choose between two options: accept the proposed division or reject it. In the event of a refusal, both parties would lose everything. Each of us wrote an offer on a piece of paper. The "right" answer in utilitarian
terms was given by the only business and management student in the classroom: he offered one coin, confident that was the best solution to maximize both players' individual utility (i.e., the other would rather keep one than go home with zero). None of the social economy students offered less than 50%. Teach neoliberal capitalism uncritically, exacerbate inequality; teach diversity in economics, generate fairer societies.
### Ecosystem Regeneration
Finally, questioning taken-for-granted assumptions includes interrogating wider understandings of management as a mechanistic discipline. Rather than cogs in a machine, interacting but separate, the environment, society, and business need to be considered as interdependent elements of a complex living system ([Capra, 1982](#page-13-0)). Such world-view redefinition implies discarding "the engineer's hard hat" and donning "a pair of gardening gloves" instead ([Raworth, 2017](#page-16-0): 130). That is, it requires equipping students with the ability to understand the basic principles of ecology and subsequently design organizations in ways that promote ecological flourishing; with the confidence to implement these design decisions; and with the wisdom to approach them in light of the organized complexity in which they are embedded, aware of the interdependency between environment, society, and business. Therefore, a system approach to management requires a transformation of the business school curricula, to develop stronger interdisciplinarity and transdisciplinarity (which differ from multidisciplinarity and antidisciplinarity [see[ Choi & Pak, 2006](#page-13-0);[ Ergene et al., 2021;](#page-13-0) [Griffiths, 2022]](#page-14-0)). An interdisciplinary curriculum links up different disciplines to generate a coherent dialogue around common themes [(Choi & Pak, 2006;](#page-13-0) [Schipper, Dubash, & Mulugetta, 2021](#page-16-0)). This is the case, for example, in social science and natural science departments working together in creating joint degree programs. A transdisciplinary curriculum transcends the traditional boundaries between disciplines ([Choi & Pak, 2006)](#page-13-0), including learning pathways that fully integrate different subjects—for example, scientists across the university that collaborate to teach climate change in the Anthropocene ([Leichenko & O](#page-15-0)'Brien, 2020), and business and bioscience scholars that work together to teach ecological economics. Considering economic activities as constituted by social relations and limited by the biocapacity of the Earth, ecological economics involves understanding the foundations of both economics
and ecology and allows for applying ecological principles to economic studies [(Costanza, 1992)](#page-13-0).
While a mechanistic approach to management, based on colonial legacies and related exploitative human–nature relationships, results in eco-illiteracy and the overshooting of planetary boundaries, a system approach has the potential to create ecological awareness and restore the ecosystem upon which our livelihoods depend ([Banerjee & Arjali](#page-12-0)es, 2021; [Ergene et al., 2021)](#page-13-0). According to[ Capra (1996),](#page-13-0) eco-literacy (i.e. the ability to understand basic ecological principles) is key to enable the creation of sustainable human communities, inclusive of sustainable economies. For example, the ability to understand the cyclical processes of nature (e.g., the carbon cycle, nitrogen cycle, water cycle, and so on) and appreciate their importance for human survival can support the design of circular businesses ([Raworth, 2017](#page-16-0)). A business that is "regenerative by design" is "generous": it explicitly aims to enrich the living systems of which it is a part [(Raworth, 2017:](#page-16-0) 218). In addition, the ability to comprehend how the economy is an open system, embedded in a finite and closed ecosystem, enables understanding of the importance of limits in conducting economic activities, problematizing the pursuit of infinite economic growth in a planet with finite resources and appreciating the goals of "sustainable scale" and "fair distribution" alongside "efficient allocation" [(Daly,](#page-13-0) [1996)](#page-13-0).
Adopting a system approach to management allows for designing a business school that is symbiotic with the ecosystem that supports it, including the local community. For example, the University of Bologna, in Italy, encourages students to inhabit the community and be actively involved in it through facilitating home-sharing between university students and local residents—senior citizens in particular. The initiative, called "Grandparents adopt students" [(Nonni adottano studenti, 2015](#page-15-0)), helps the elderly overcome social isolation, provides students with affordable accommodations, and improves social cohesion in cities. When adopting a system approach, everything in the civic business school aims to overcome the separation (and consequent exclusion) of commercial life from the rest of life.
After having unpacked the process through which contemporary management education yields dysfunctional outcomes, and having proposed to reconfigure it around the principles of CME, by exploring their functions, in the next section I will advance some possible strategies to enhance CME in practice.
### DOING CIVIC MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
The marketization and commodification of higher education create powerful pressures on students, academics, and administrators alike to act in conformity to the neoliberal "common sense," rather than nourishing critical thinking and exploring new possibilities. In this context, how can the positive potential of CME be fulfilled?
[Merton (1948](#page-15-0): 209) suggested that "deliberate institutional change" is needed to enable virtuous cycles. The first item on a civic policy agenda should be redefining the "why"—that is, changing the goal from the attainment of individual benefits and private economic aspirations to the pursuit of ecological flourishing. Students have a key role to play. Through rethinking the "why" behind their choice of study, they can provide crucial pressure to reframe higher education as a public and common good. In practice, unless tuition fees are waived or calculated according to income and asset levels, students will likely continue to view their education in instrumental terms (as an investment toward a profitable career). The second item on the civic agenda should be redefining the "who" (e.g., who inhabits the business school). In recent years, initiatives promoting justice, equality, diversity and inclusion have become very popular, in light of the array of studies that have demonstrated how diversity generates positive outcomes, including improved financial performance and revenue growth [(Hunt, Yee, Prince, &](#page-14-0) [Dixon-Fyle, 2018](#page-14-0)). However, they have barely scratched the surface of entrenched inequality ([Pathak, 2021)](#page-16-0). Unless business schools are redesigned as distributive organizations, changing their governance structure around increased transparency and enhanced cooperative management, they are likely to remain a boys' club. As[ Locatelli (2018: 12)](#page-15-0) remarked: "Empowering communities to make important decisions about the institutions in which they live is probably the most effective way to make educational opportunities and governance more sustainable and equitable." The third item should be redefining the "what" (e.g., what to learn and teach). This involves giving more autonomy to faculty members to adapt the curriculum to local and global challenges and to change the syllabus to enhance critical and systemic thinking, introducing issues of social and environmental justice, repositioning "who and what gets to occupy the center and the margins of ideas and societies" [(Kerval, 2019](#page-14-0): para. 2), and designing programs and modules of study around what matters rather than what sells. In practice, as
long as institutional choices are guided by the market only, and unless they allow a lower student-toteacher ratio, incorporating CME principles in learning and teaching will be extremely difficult. The fourth item on the civic agenda should be redefining the "how." To counter the neoliberal obsession with quantitative measures, the civic university should encourage qualitative experiences and "stop competing on rankings" designed around the maximization of individual utility [(Podolny, 2009](#page-16-0): 67). Quantitative measures do not always provide proof of quality ([Hutt, 2021)](#page-14-0); on the contrary, sometimes they strip learning experiences of their meaning. For example, take the latest digital learning platforms, developed as part of the recent shift to online teaching, which have the ambition of measuring students' interactions. As one's personal score rises in relation to, for instance, the number of comments written in a chat and the number of polls joined, students compete to be the most "active" user, rather than learning together in a free, spontaneous, and respectful environment. On the other hand, the value of rich, meaningful, and transformative learning experiences cannot be easily captured in quantitative terms ([Maisuria & Cole, 2017)](#page-15-0). Unless performance pressures are reduced, the culture of competition will hardly be uprooted, and both students and academics will continue to experience poor mental health and an ever-worsening quality of education. Such a transformation requires support from a wide range of internal and external stakeholders (e.g., students, academics, professional services, graduate employers, local and global initiatives, etc.). Importantly, it requires the government to be on board, which, in a democracy, requires citizens to be actively involved.
While policy-driven institutional change is necessary, it is not the only way forward.[ Gibson-Graham](#page-14-0)'s [(2006)](#page-14-0) research on diverse economies has suggested that there are at least three more ways to enhance CME in practice, complementary and preparatory to policy change. These include cultivating "a politics of language," "a politics of the subject' and "a politics of collective action" [(Gibson-Graham, 2006:](#page-14-0) ix–xviii). Cultivating a politics of language means "developing new, richer local languages of economy and economic possibility" [(Gibson-Graham, 2006:](#page-14-0) xi). For example, through dialogue with ecology, economics develops a new language around the concepts of sustainable scale and fair distribution ([Daly, 1996)](#page-13-0), which allows for the inclusion of planetary boundaries and social and environmental justice in the business school curricula. As thinking economy differently allows for creating different economies
([Gibson-Graham, 2006](#page-14-0): xii), thinking business education differently allows for creating different business schools.
Cultivating a politics of the subject means nourishing ourselves and others as free agents of change ([Gibson-Graham, 2006](#page-14-0): xv). This involves personal resistance, embodying change within and outside the classroom (e.g., practicing intellectual activism, prioritizing ecological and human flourishing over individual status and reward, cultivating civic capabilities, reducing working hours, sharing more, etc.). A politics of the subject requires developing critical consciousness. This is what[ Freire (1970](#page-13-0): 9) defined as "conscientizac¸ao~ ," [Lindebaum (2017:](#page-15-0) 61) as "seeing things through" and[ Fleming (2021b](#page-13-0): 18) as "self-consciousness." In other words, it requires developing the ability to recognize vicious cycles and the harmful consequences they generate on the environment, society, and business; to realize how we are individually and collectively affected by these dysfunctions; and to take action for human and ecological flourishing, accepting our role and responsibility to make change happen. In the classroom, a politics of the subject can be pursued through introducing teaching methods such as roleplay, "forum-theater" and other workshops in which students can embody, analyze, and transform the reality in which they live [(Boal, 1993)](#page-13-0).
Cultivating a politics of collective action means "working collaboratively to produce alternative economic organizations and spaces in place" ([Gibson-](#page-14-0)[Graham, 2006:](#page-14-0) xvii). This is enabled through networks and partnerships that stimulate mutual support. For example, networks of early-career researchers who actively resist neoliberal management education help in overcoming "occupational fear" [(Fleming,](#page-13-0) [2021b)](#page-13-0), support individual struggles, and strengthen solidarity. Networks and partnerships can be formal or informal (or both), wide in reach or localized, and positioned outside or within the mainstream [(Parker](#page-16-0) [et al., 2014)](#page-16-0). Most importantly, they require trust which presupposes recognition of the trustworthiness of others.
# CONCLUSION
The dysfunctional effects of neoliberal management education are destroying our common home. As[ Parker](#page-16-0) [(2021](#page-16-0), par. 5) remarked, "The problem is that the global b-school industry has consequences for all of us and allowing it to continue selling get rich quick schemes is endangering the future of life on this planet. It's that simple." The present essay offers two theoretical
contributions to the debate about transforming higher education ([Cottom, 2017; Fleming, 2021b](#page-13-0);[ Hill, 2012;](#page-14-0) [Murphy, 2017](#page-15-0);[ Newfield, 2018)](#page-15-0), and the business school in particular [(Fotaki & Prasad, 2015](#page-13-0);[ Grey, 2004;](#page-14-0) [Kitchener & Delbridge, 2020;](#page-15-0)[ Parker, 2018](#page-16-0);[ Tourish,](#page-16-0) [2020](#page-16-0);[Wang et al., 2011](#page-16-0)).
First, through the use of functional explanations, the essay unpacks the process through which selfinterest, instrumental rationality, capitalist organizing, and a mechanistic approach to management yield dysfunctional outcomes (including the normalization and reproduction of greed, the creation of instrumental business schools, the exacerbation of inequality, and ecosystem degradation). In other words, it exposes the self-harming process that leads to the "autoimmunity" of the business school [(van](#page-16-0) [Houtum & van Uden, 2022)](#page-16-0). Only after the process that generates dysfunctional outcomes is uncovered is it possible to subvert it, moving beyond critique and "decoding" the process that can potentially enable the business school to heal ([Merton, 1948](#page-15-0)). In light of this, the essay proposes that we reconfigure management education around generalized reciprocity, substantive rationality, diverse organizing, and a system approach to management, suggesting that this has the potential to produce functional outcomes (including the nourishment of cooperative humans, substantive business schools, income and wealth distribution, and ecosystem regeneration).
Second, the essay calls for a new paradigmatic orientation to civility. While the current civic university agenda is narrowly focused on civic engagement [(Brink, 2018; Civic University Network, n.d.;](#page-13-0) [Goodard, 2009](#page-14-0)) and essentially anthropocentric ([Bruni](#page-13-0) [& Zamagni, 2007)](#page-13-0), this essay proposes a reformulation of civility from a radical system perspective—one that illuminates the impact of management studies on the ecosystem that supports it, addresses the interdependence of natural and social systems, and redesigns management education in ways that enable ecological and human flourishing (Banerjee & Arjalies, 2021; [Ergene et al., 2021](#page-13-0)).
When confronted with the dysfunctional consequences of neoliberal management education, it is easy to resign to the "spectralization" of higher education [(Fleming, 2021b](#page-13-0)), but believing that all is lost means losing everything indeed. This itself is a selffulfilling prophecy. On the other hand, focusing on what makes academia a place of emancipation and nourishing that transformative potential, is, I believe, the way forward. "Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will" (Antonini, 2019: 42): only hope brings about transformation. In summary,
I propose that civility—approached systemically—is the direction in which management education should point its compass, the horizon toward which we should walk.
In stark contrast to the neoliberal project, which is built on self-interest and private accumulation, "civilizing" the business school—from the Latin civilis, or "relating to public life" [(Online Etymology](#page-15-0) [Dictionary, n.d.)](#page-15-0)—requires refocusing the purpose of higher education around public and common good, reconnecting ecology with political economy, and reimagining human–nature relationships based on the interdependence between the environment, society, and business. We are surrounded by powerful examples of human cooperation, regenerative enterprise, and substantive resistance. It is time to learn to see, refuse the inevitability of human and ecological collapse, and work together to take care of our collective home.
